title: The economy: a wave moving through time

steps.title: From the universe to an economy
steps.text: The blue level ends in nations. Open one, the United States, and the same cause-and-effect logic continues: like the food chain, every business feeds on the layers beneath it, down to the government it all stands on.

steps.title: A wave moving through time
steps.text: The road of American lives since 1946 and the economy share one time axis. At now, the cross-section opens into a wave: each rib behind the crest is one year, widening as real output grows. The crest is the year shown.

steps.title: The bedrock: government
steps.text: Government is the bedrock everything stands on. In the United States it is a constitutional federal democracy. Its pillars are sized by public outlays; taxes fall into it from every household, and benefits rise out of it.

steps.title: The price of money
steps.text: The state reaches into every market through two levers: the price of money, which the central bank sets and every debt pays, and the edge of trade. Money was dearest in 1981, at 16.4% a year, and nearly free from 2009 to 2016. Tariffs fell from 7% of the value of imported goods in 1947 to under 2% in the 2010s, then tripled in 2025, from 2.6% to 8.0%.

steps.title: Other foundations
steps.text: The same hills on other states. The bedrock is as deep as what each state spends: 38% of GDP in the United States, 49% in Sweden, 33% in China, 29% in Saudi Arabia, 48% in the Soviet Union of 1980. Summits turn steel where the state controls the largest firm: in China the largest bank, oil company, power grid and telephone company, while private firms lead technology and retail. Saudi Arabia's state lives on oil: 60% of its revenue.

steps.title: Layers standing on layers
steps.text: On the bedrock, layers stand on layers: raw materials and subsistence infrastructure at the foot, then manufacturing and infrastructure, then services, with technology on top. Each industry is a ridge as wide as its share of value added.

steps.title: Companies live and die
steps.text: 75 companies live on the ridges like people on the road: born, rising and falling with market value, then failing, bought, or reaching the crest. Their color shows how they sell: meeting needs, manufactured want, or fear.

steps.title: Companies spend too
steps.text: Companies run the same program as people. A firm's year of money leaves in the directions it flows: down to its suppliers and workers, forward into the future as investment, split between desire for new demand and fear of falling behind, up to its owners, and into the state as taxes and lobbying. Arrows show which way the money moves it. In 2025 five companies spent about $450 billion building artificial intelligence, and it poured down the hill.

steps.title: Golden circles
steps.text: At every market the dollar splits: wages run back down to workers, taxes fall to the bedrock, and the surplus climbs to gold halos above the summits and to the rings of owners around the top firms - the golden circles.

steps.title: Attention above capital
steps.text: Above the capital float the most followed Americans, ringed by how many of the other most-followed follow them. Attention runs in a loop: companies pay the platforms $295 billion a year in digital advertising, the platforms and brands pay creators about $37 billion, people give about two hours a day and take in wants, and then they spend.

steps.title: Class is altitude
steps.text: Class is altitude. People live on the slope of whatever pays them, as close as possible to their source of value: an employer's industry, the government, or family wealth. The out of work sit on the valley floor; the richest float above.

steps.title: Rivers of desire and fear
steps.text: Money flows in two colors: desire, in rose, and fear, in ice. Spending runs down to each industry's market; saving leaves over the crest into the future, and debt arrives from it.

steps.title: What moves people up or down
steps.text: The hill's altitude pulled out beside the wave: five rungs of household income in 2015 and in 2025, joined by streams of people. In their working years, a lost job, a divorce and unpayable debt came with the falls; work, a child, a home and marriage with the climbs. Compared like for like, the model holds as tightly as the tax records do.

steps.title: One person
steps.text: Zoom into a single person. Where they stand on this hillside is where they stand in the social market: the slope that pays them, the rung they occupy, and the people around them.

steps.title: Inside one mind
steps.text: Inside one mind: five desire drives and five fear drives, weighed by reason into a choice. Desire pulls toward the hills that pay and please; fear pushes away from debt, loss and scarcity.

steps.title: Tit for tat
steps.text: Every encounter is a prisoner's dilemma: cooperate or defect. Tit-for-tat opens kindly, copies the partner's last move, retaliates and forgives. Over many rounds the payoffs accumulate as wealth.

steps.title: The ladder
steps.text: One life's path across the landscape over time, climbing and falling between rungs, compared with the parents' rung. Job changes, marriage, children and debt move it up or down.

steps.title: Groups play the same game
steps.text: Groups play the same game as people: cooperation, retaliation and forgiveness between groups and tribes. Coalitions form where cooperation keeps paying, and break where it does not.

steps.title: Where do you stand?
steps.text: Tell the model about your household in the panel. It places you among the year's simulated Americans: your rung on the hill you work on, where each dollar you spend goes and which way its income flows, how far you are from living on what you own, and where people like you were ten years later. Nothing you enter is kept.

steps.title: Somewhere on this hillside
steps.text: Back to the whole wave. The economy is the newest layer of the same causal chain that began with the Big Bang - and you are somewhere on this hillside, moving with it into the future.
